title: THE CLOSER THEY GET TO RELIGION, THE FARTHER THEY GET FROM THE HEART OF JESUS
paragraphs: THE CLOSER THEY GET TO RELIGION, THE FARTHER THEY GET FROM THE HEART OF JESUS
Why Do Some Christians Become More Religious but Less Compassionate? The Frightening Truth About Knowing Scripture, Defending Holiness, and Slowly Forgetting How to Love People
There is a kind of Christian who can recognize sin from across the room but cannot recognize a wounded soul standing right in front of them.

They know the commandments. They defend sound doctrine. They attend church faithfully. They can quote Scripture, expose false teaching, correct theological errors, and explain why the world desperately needs repentance.
But somehow, somewhere along the journey, their patience became shorter. Their words became sharper. Their judgments became quicker.
And their compassion became harder to find.
They can spend hours arguing about biblical truth but struggle to spend five minutes listening to someone whose life has fallen apart.
They can passionately defend the holiness of marriage while humiliating a woman who survived a broken one.
They can preach forgiveness while refusing to forgive someone who wounded them years ago.
They can celebrate the grace that rescued them while treating another person's failures as proof that they deserve rejection.
And perhaps the most frightening part?
They may genuinely believe they are becoming more like Jesus.
But before we point toward someone else, there is a question we must allow the Holy Spirit to bring painfully close to home.
What if the person slowly losing compassion is you?
What if it is me?
What if we have become so occupied with being right that we have forgotten what it means to love rightly?
Because there is something deeply unsettling in the Gospels.
Some of the people who knew the Scriptures most thoroughly were among those who opposed Jesus most fiercely.
And some of the people whose lives were publicly stained by sin were the very people who recognized their desperate need for Him.

That should make every believer tremble—not because studying Scripture is dangerous, but because knowing sacred words without surrendering to the One they reveal can leave a human heart frighteningly unchanged.
Jesus once confronted religious leaders with words that still cut through centuries of church history.

In Matthew 23:23, He rebuked certain scribes and Pharisees for carefully giving a tenth of their spices while neglecting what He called the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
Notice something extraordinary.
Jesus did not tell them that obedience was unimportant.
He told them they had neglected something essential while concentrating on something else.
They were meticulous about measurable religious duties, yet careless about the moral character those duties were supposed to cultivate.
They could count the smallest portions of their offerings.
But they had lost sight of the suffering of human beings.
They could measure religious performance.
But mercy had become almost invisible.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because the same danger exists today.
A person can faithfully give money to a church and still mistreat their family.
A person can refuse worldly entertainment and still entertain cruelty in their heart.
A person can defend biblical marriage and still speak contemptuously to their spouse.
A person can memorize the Sermon on the Mount while refusing to live its simplest commands.
Religious activity can increase while spiritual maturity remains stagnant.
Not because prayer, worship, giving, or obedience are wrong.
They are precious gifts when offered to God sincerely.
But when those practices become substitutes for humility, love, repentance, and dependence upon Christ, something has gone terribly wrong.
And Jesus never intended His followers to confuse the appearance of holiness with the fruit of holiness.
The Greek word translated "mercy" in Matthew 23:23 is ἔλεος (eleos).
It carries the sense of mercy or compassion shown toward someone in need.
It is not merely feeling sorry for someone from a comfortable distance.
It is the kind of concern that refuses to treat another person's suffering as irrelevant.
The Greek word κρίσις (krisis), translated "justice" or "judgment" depending on context, points here toward the righteous and just treatment of others.
Jesus placed justice and mercy among the weightier matters of the law.
Not optional decorations.
Not sentimental extras.
Weightier matters.
And yet how easily we reverse the priorities.
We become passionate about correcting other people's behavior while neglecting to examine the condition of our own hearts.
We become experts at identifying what is wrong with the world while remaining strangers to the pride growing inside us.
We become defenders of truth who forget that the Truth Himself knelt to wash His disciples' feet.
Think about that for a moment.
The Son of God, who possessed all authority, wrapped a towel around His waist and served people who still misunderstood Him.
He even washed the feet of Judas, knowing the betrayal that was coming.
That was not weakness.
That was holiness expressed through humble love.
And if our understanding of holiness makes us increasingly incapable of humble love, we should question whether we are becoming more like Christ or merely more impressed with ourselves.
There is a story in Luke 18:9–14 that exposes this danger with almost unbearable precision.
Jesus described two men who went to the temple to pray.
One was a Pharisee.
The other was a tax collector.
In that society, the Pharisee represented serious religious observance. The tax collector belonged to a profession widely associated with exploitation and betrayal.
The Pharisee stood and thanked God that he was not like other people.
He mentioned his fasting.
He mentioned his tithing.
He mentioned his moral distinctions.
His prayer sounded religious.
But it revealed a heart comparing itself with others.
The tax collector stood at a distance.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beat his chest and pleaded:
"God, be merciful to me, a sinner." (Luke 18:13, KJV)
The original Greek contains a remarkable expression:
Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
Ho Theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō.
A close translation is:
"God, be merciful to me, the sinner."
The verb hilasthēti comes from language associated with atonement and the turning away of divine wrath. The tax collector was not merely asking God to overlook his behavior.
He was appealing to God's mercy because he knew he had no righteousness of his own to present as a bargaining chip.
One man stood before God with a list of achievements.
The other stood before God with a confession.
And Jesus declared that the tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee.
Not because sin was suddenly acceptable.
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
But because God justifies the humble sinner who depends upon His mercy, not the self-righteous person who trusts in his own religious performance.
Here is the uncomfortable question.
When was the last time we approached God without quietly comparing ourselves to somebody we considered worse?
When was the last time we confessed our sins without immediately thinking about somebody else's?
When was the last time we prayed for someone who embarrassed the church instead of simply talking about how badly they embarrassed it?
Sometimes the most dangerous words a Christian can whisper are not openly rebellious words.
Sometimes they are:
"At least I'm not like them."
Because the moment another person's failure becomes the foundation of our spiritual confidence, we have already wandered away from the foot of the cross.
And the cross leaves no room for spiritual superiority.
It reminds every believer that salvation is not a trophy awarded to the morally impressive.
It is grace given to sinners through Jesus Christ.
Paul wrote in Ephesians 2:8–9 that salvation is by grace through faith, not from ourselves and not by works, so that no one may boast.
No one.
Not the lifelong church member.
Not the respected pastor.
Not the gifted Bible teacher.
Not the person whose testimony seems cleaner than everyone else's.
Every redeemed soul stands before God because of Christ's mercy.
And when we forget that, compassion begins to disappear.
Because we start treating grace as something we once needed rather than something upon which we still depend.
But why does this happen?
Why can someone become increasingly involved in religion while becoming less patient, less gentle, and less compassionate?
Sometimes it begins with fear.
Fear of compromise.
Fear of false teaching.
Fear that showing kindness to a sinner will somehow communicate approval of sin.
And that fear can gradually produce a false choice.
Truth or love.
Holiness or mercy.
Conviction or compassion.
But Jesus never made us choose between those things.
John 1:14 describes Him as full of grace and truth.
Not half grace and half truth.
Full of both.
He did not dilute God's holiness to make people comfortable.
And He did not abandon compassion to prove He was holy.
He could confront sin without treating sinners as disposable.
He could expose hypocrisy without becoming hypocritical.
He could speak hard truths while genuinely seeking the salvation of those who heard Him.
Consider the woman brought before Him in John 8.
Her accusers placed her in the center of public attention.
Her sin had become a spectacle.
Her shame had become an argument.
They wanted a verdict.
Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of her accusers and refused to condemn her.
Then He told her to leave her life of sin.
There was no celebration of adultery.
There was no denial that wrongdoing mattered.
But neither was there permission to use a wounded human being as an instrument of religious cruelty.
Jesus upheld righteousness without surrendering mercy.
And this matters enormously.
Because compassion does not mean calling evil good.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending abuse never happened.
Grace does not mean eliminating accountability.
Love does not mean allowing someone to continue harming others without consequences.
A compassionate church can confront sin, protect victims, practice appropriate discipline, establish boundaries, and pursue restoration wherever genuine repentance makes restoration possible.
Biblical compassion is not moral confusion.
It is the refusal to stop seeing a human being as someone made in God's image, even when that person has done wrong.
That distinction can change everything.
Imagine a young woman sitting near the back of a church.
She has not attended worship in months.
Her relationship collapsed. Her family is disappointed. Rumors have traveled faster than her explanations.
She finally gathers enough courage to walk through the doors.
She does not need someone to tell her that every decision she made was acceptable.
She knows she has made mistakes.
She needs the truth.
But she also needs to know whether the people preaching about grace have any grace left for someone like her.
Now imagine that the first thing she encounters is a whisper.
A stare.
A conversation that stops when she approaches.
A smile that feels more like suspicion than welcome.
And she quietly wonders whether coming back was a mistake.
We cannot know every hidden struggle in the people who enter our churches.
But we can know what Jesus commands of us.
We can speak truth.
We can listen.
We can refuse gossip.
We can welcome the repentant.
We can offer help without demanding that wounded people first become impressive enough to deserve our attention.
And we can remember that the church is not a gathering of people who have never needed rescue.
It is a people who confess that their only ultimate hope is the crucified and risen Christ.
Some Christians become less compassionate because they have begun to confuse separation from sin with separation from sinners.
But Jesus was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners.
He ate with people whom religious society considered disgraceful.
In Mark 2:17, He explained that He had come not to call the righteous, but sinners.
This did not mean He approved of their wrongdoing.
It meant their wrongdoing was precisely why they needed a Savior.
A physician does not prove his commitment to health by refusing to enter a room filled with sick people.
And a church does not prove its commitment to holiness by treating every struggling sinner as a contamination risk.
Holiness is not the absence of compassion.
True holiness reflects the character of the holy God.
And the God revealed in Scripture is both righteous and merciful.
In Exodus 34:6–7, the Lord reveals Himself as compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, while also refusing to treat guilt as morally insignificant.
The Hebrew word רַחוּם (raḥum) means "compassionate" or "merciful."
The word חַנּוּן (ḥannun) means "gracious."
And חֶסֶד (ḥesed) speaks of steadfast love, covenant loyalty, or faithful kindness, depending on its context.
These are not qualities that God reluctantly borrows when He feels sentimental.
They belong to His revealed character.
He is holy.
He is just.
He is compassionate.
He is gracious.
And if our spirituality increasingly reflects severity without mercy, we are not displaying the fullness of His character.
We are displaying a distortion.
There is another reason compassion sometimes fades.
Pride can disguise itself as discernment.
And this is especially dangerous because discernment is genuinely necessary.
Christians are commanded to test teaching, distinguish truth from error, and refuse what contradicts the Gospel.
But biblical discernment requires humility.
It must begin with submission to Scripture and an awareness of our own fallibility.
Prideful discernment begins somewhere else.
It begins with the secret satisfaction of finding someone to correct.
Eventually, a person may stop asking, "How can I help this person understand the truth?"
And begin asking, "How can I prove this person wrong?"
The difference may be invisible to an audience.
But God sees the heart.
Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 8:1:
"Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth." (KJV)
The Greek expression behind "puffeth up" is φυσιοῖ (physioi), meaning "puffs up" or "makes arrogant."
And the word translated "charity" in the King James Version is ἀγάπη (agapē), love.
Paul was not condemning knowledge itself.
He was warning that knowledge without love can produce arrogance, while love builds others up.
Think about how often this plays out in Christian conversations.
Someone asks a sincere question.
Instead of receiving patient instruction, they receive ridicule.
Someone misunderstands a doctrine.
Instead of being gently corrected, they are publicly embarrassed.
Someone admits spiritual confusion.
Instead of finding a brother or sister willing to walk with them, they are treated as a threat.
And eventually, people become afraid to admit what they do not understand.
Afraid to confess what they are struggling with.
Afraid to ask for prayer.
Afraid to say they are hurting.
Not because the Gospel is cruel.
But because some of us have forgotten how to communicate its truth with the gentleness Scripture requires.
Second Timothy 2:24–25 teaches that the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome, but kind, able to teach, patient when wronged, and gentle in correcting opponents.
Notice that Paul did not eliminate correction.
He described the character required of the person doing the correcting.
The truth matters.
And the manner in which we communicate it matters too.
We cannot excuse cruelty by calling it courage.
We cannot excuse arrogance by calling it boldness.
And we cannot excuse contempt by calling it spiritual maturity.
Jesus spoke with authority unlike anyone else.
Yet He also welcomed children, touched lepers, fed hungry crowds, wept at a friend's tomb, and restored a disciple who had denied Him.
He was never morally compromised.
And He was never spiritually indifferent.
His love was holy.
His holiness was loving.
And the more we grow into His likeness, the less comfortable we should become with our own pride.
Perhaps you have experienced the painful side of this.
Perhaps you once trusted a Christian who seemed deeply spiritual.
You opened up about your marriage.
Your addiction.
Your past.
Your doubts.
Your grief.
And instead of finding patient biblical counsel, you became the subject of somebody else's conversation.
Perhaps the person who knew the most Bible verses was the person whose words hurt you most.
Perhaps you walked away from a church gathering feeling smaller, dirtier, and more hopeless than when you arrived.
If that happened, the cruelty you experienced should not be excused as biblical faithfulness.
But neither should the failures of Christians be mistaken for the character of Christ.
Jesus is not a reflection of our worst religious behavior.
He is the perfect revelation of the Father.
And He is the standard by which every church, teacher, leader, and believer must be examined.
There is room to acknowledge spiritual wounds without abandoning the truth of the Gospel.
There is room to pursue healing without pretending that all Christians are hypocrites.
And there is room to forgive while still establishing wise boundaries and seeking justice when wrongdoing has occurred.
But there is also a difficult truth for those of us who have been hurt.
We must be careful that another person's hardness does not slowly become our own.
Because wounded people can become guarded.
Guarded people can become suspicious.
And suspicion, if left unchecked, can turn into contempt.
Suddenly, we begin treating everyone who reminds us of our pain as though they are guilty of the same offense.
This is why we need the healing work of Christ.
Not merely to make us feel better.
But to keep our wounds from becoming weapons.
There is a moment in Luke 10 that every religious person should revisit.
A man is traveling from Jerusalem to Jericho.
He is attacked by robbers.
Beaten.
Stripped.
Left half dead.
A priest sees him and passes by.
A Levite also sees him and passes by.
Then a Samaritan approaches.
To the original audience, this detail was startling because Jews and Samaritans had a history of deep hostility.
Yet it is the Samaritan who stops.
He approaches the wounded man.
Treats his injuries.
Places him on his own animal.
Brings him to an inn.
And provides for his care.
Jesus told this parable in response to a question about loving one's neighbor.
The religious identities of the priest and Levite did not guarantee merciful action.
And the Samaritan's socially despised identity did not prevent him from demonstrating genuine neighborly love.
The story exposes the distance that can exist between religious status and obedient compassion.
And here is a question worth carrying into every church service.
How many wounded people have we passed while rushing toward another religious responsibility?
How many lonely people have we overlooked while discussing ministry plans?
How many exhausted parents have we judged without understanding the burdens they carry?
How many struggling young believers have we dismissed because their questions made us uncomfortable?
How many people have we condemned in conversations when we could have prayed for them instead?
The Samaritan did not begin by investigating whether the injured man deserved help.
He recognized suffering and responded with mercy.
Jesus concluded the parable by telling His listener to go and do likewise.
Not simply to admire compassion.
Not merely to preach about compassion.
To practice it.
And that is where our theology must eventually become visible.
In how we speak to the person who disagrees with us.
In how we treat the believer who has fallen.
In how we respond when someone confesses a shameful struggle.
In how we speak about people who are not present to defend themselves.
In how we treat our families after the worship service ends.
Because one of the most revealing tests of spiritual maturity is not how passionately we speak about Jesus in public.
It is how faithfully we reflect His character when there is no audience.
And if that thought stings, perhaps it is supposed to.
Not to drive us into despair.
But to lead us into repentance.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
The Holy Spirit convicts us of sin and directs us toward Christ.
Self-righteous condemnation often leaves us staring at ourselves or despising others.
The Gospel does something better.
It tells the truth about our sin.
Then it points us toward the Savior who died and rose again.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love toward us in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became respectable.
Not after we cleaned up our reputations.
Not after we mastered theological vocabulary.
Christ died for the ungodly.
And when that truth settles deeply into the soul, it becomes harder to look at another struggling human being with contempt.
Because we remember the mercy that found us.
We remember the sins nobody else knew about.
We remember the prayers we whispered when we were ashamed.
We remember the moments when we had no defense except the grace of God.
And suddenly, the person we were tempted to dismiss begins to look less like an enemy and more like someone who needs the same Savior who rescued us.
This is not moral relativism.
This is Gospel humility.
And Gospel humility does not weaken holiness.
It strengthens obedience by placing it where it belongs—as the fruit of grace rather than the price of acceptance before God.
Paul wrote in Galatians 6:1 that believers who are spiritual should restore someone caught in transgression with a spirit of gentleness, watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
The Greek word translated "restore" is καταρτίζετε (katartizete), from katartizō, a verb used for putting something in order, mending, or restoring.
The instruction is not to celebrate the transgression.
It is to pursue restoration.
And the restoration must be carried out gently.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the person doing the restoring is also vulnerable to temptation.
That last part matters.
The one offering correction must remember their own weakness.
A believer who remembers their vulnerability is less likely to treat another person's failure as entertainment.
Less likely to gossip.
Less likely to humiliate.
Less likely to confuse public embarrassment with genuine repentance.
And more likely to ask the question that compassion always brings to the surface:
"How can I help this person move toward Christ?"
Not how can I win?
Not how can I look superior?
Not how can I make an example of them?
How can I help them move toward Christ?
Sometimes that will mean speaking an uncomfortable truth.
Sometimes it will mean calling someone to repent.
Sometimes it will mean reporting wrongdoing, protecting those at risk, or refusing to enable destructive behavior.
And sometimes it will mean sitting quietly beside someone whose heart is too exhausted to hear another lecture.
Wisdom knows that different wounds require different kinds of care.
Love refuses to abandon truth.
And truth must never be used as an excuse to abandon love.
Perhaps the most devastating warning comes from the words of Jesus Himself.
In John 13:35, He said:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." (KJV)
He did not say the world would recognize His disciples primarily by their ability to win arguments.
Or by their impressive religious vocabulary.
Or by their flawless public image.
He pointed to their love for one another.
The Greek word is again ἀγάπη (agapē).
In this passage, it describes the love Jesus commands His disciples to demonstrate toward each other.
Not a shallow agreement that ignores wrongdoing.
Not emotional affection that disappears when relationships become difficult.
But a love shaped by the self-giving example of Christ.
A love that serves.
A love that tells the truth.
A love that seeks another person's good.
A love that can endure inconvenience.
A love that remembers how much it has been forgiven.
And this raises a sobering possibility.
Some people may know what Christians oppose without ever experiencing the kind of love Jesus said would identify His followers.
That should grieve us.
Because the Gospel is too glorious to be obscured by our arrogance.
And Christ is too worthy to be represented by a faith that speaks of redemption while delighting in humiliation.
The answer is not to become less biblical.
It is to become more deeply biblical.
To read Scripture not merely as ammunition for arguments but as God's Word that exposes our own hearts.
To pursue sound doctrine and the fruit of the Spirit.
To practice holiness and mercy.
To love truth and love people.
To confront sin while remembering that we ourselves live by grace.
James 2:13 gives a particularly serious warning:
"For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment." (KJV)
James is not teaching that acts of compassion purchase salvation.
He is warning that mercilessness is profoundly inconsistent with the faith believers profess.
A heart genuinely transformed by God's mercy should increasingly become merciful.
Not perfectly.
Not instantly.
But visibly, over time, through the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit.
And Galatians 5:22–23 tells us what the fruit of the Spirit includes.
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Patience.
Kindness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Gentleness.
Self-control.
These qualities matter.
They are not signs of theological weakness.
They are evidence of the Spirit's transforming work.
A Christian may become more knowledgeable without becoming more mature.
But a Christian growing in genuine Christlikeness should not be content to remain cruel.
The closer we walk with Jesus, the more seriously we should take both His truth and His command to love.
So what happens if you recognize yourself in this article?
What if you realize you have been harsh?
What if you have used biblical language to disguise impatience?
What if you have enjoyed exposing someone else's failure?
What if you have demanded grace from God while withholding compassion from people?
There is good news.
You do not have to defend the person you have become.
You can repent.
You can confess the pride.
You can apologize to the people you wounded.
You can stop spreading the story that was never yours to tell.
You can ask God to soften the places in your heart that have grown hard.
You can return to the Scriptures with a different prayer.
Not merely, "Lord, show me what is wrong with everyone else."
But, "Lord, search me."
"Correct me."
"Teach me."
"Make me more like Jesus."
And when the Spirit exposes sin, do not run from Christ in shame.
Run toward Him in repentance and faith.
The same Savior who confronted the pride of religious leaders also received repentant sinners.
The same Jesus who called people to turn away from sin gave His life to save sinners.
He was crucified for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
And through Him, forgiveness and new life are proclaimed.
That is the Gospel.
Not the promise that God will applaud our religious achievements.
But the astonishing announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
And those who belong to Him are called to walk in the newness of life His grace produces.
Maybe you have spent years becoming better at defending Christianity.
Now ask God to make you better at displaying Christ.
Maybe you have learned how to identify false teaching.
Now ask Him to help you identify the pride in your own heart.
Maybe you have learned how to speak firmly.
Now ask Him to teach you when to listen tenderly.
Maybe you have become so afraid of compromising truth that you have forgotten how to welcome a person who desperately needs it.
Come back to Jesus.
Not to a softer Gospel.
Not to a Gospel without repentance.
But to the real Gospel.
The Gospel in which holiness and mercy meet at the cross.
The Gospel in which sin is serious enough to require the death of the Son of God, and grace is glorious enough to offer forgiveness to those who repent and believe.
The Gospel that does not leave us as we were.
The Gospel that transforms proud hearts into humble ones.
Hard hearts into tender ones.
Self-righteous hearts into grateful ones.
And wounded people into people who, by God's grace, can learn to love again.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create another gathering of people who merely know Christian terminology.
But to help believers and seekers encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discernment, practice repentance, and mature in their walk with Jesus Christ.
We want truth that reaches beyond the screen.
Truth that enters our homes.
Truth that changes how we speak to our children.
Truth that changes how we treat our spouses.
Truth that teaches us to forgive, serve, endure, and love without compromising the Word of God.
And if this article has challenged you, please do not allow it to become just another post you read and forget.
You do not need to expose private details or name people who hurt you.
And if you know you have become harder toward people than you once were, perhaps today is the day to write:
Your words may encourage someone else to stop pretending, seek prayer, and begin an honest journey of repentance and healing.
A single share may bring this message to someone who has quietly concluded that Christianity has no room for broken people.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable.
But because there may come a day when you need to remember that winning an argument is not the same thing as winning a person through faithful, Christlike witness.
If you want to help this ministry continue and expand, there is another meaningful way to participate.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that believers should give willingly rather than under pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
We want to honor both truths.

It can help us continue producing content for people who are spiritually exhausted, those searching for biblical answers, believers recovering from painful seasons, and Christians who want to grow beyond religious routine into a deeper walk with Jesus.
These resources are intended to encourage faith, reflection, and Gospel-centered conversations in everyday life.
The heart behind these resources is simple: biblical nourishment should be accessible, and the Word of God should remain central.
Both can matter.
Both can be offered with sincere love.
And neither should ever be driven by guilt.
Stay rooted in His Word.
Stay faithful to the Gospel.
And never allow your knowledge of God to become an excuse for refusing to reflect His compassion.
Because at the end of this journey, the question is not merely how many verses we memorized, how many arguments we won, how many religious activities we attended, or how many people we corrected.
The question is whether our lives increasingly bear witness to the Lord we claim to follow.
May we be people who defend truth without becoming cruel.
People who practice holiness without becoming proud.
People who confront sin without forgetting grace.
People who love deeply without abandoning conviction.
And people who never forget that we are standing today only because Jesus Christ had mercy on us.
May the people who encounter us never have to recover from our religion before they can recognize the compassion of our Savior.
